summary: The second list of socket numbers assigned for public functions on the early ARPANET, expanded to include more experimental sockets and new assignments for standard, host-specific and experimental functions. It describes the 40-bit socket structure. It obsoletes RFC 433 and was replaced by RFC 739.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 503 lists socket numbers assigned to network services and shows which hosts offer them. It replaced RFC 433 and was later replaced by RFC 739.

questions: which services had assigned socket numbers
subtitle: A registry of socket numbers and the network services assigned to them

tldr.problem: Network users and programs needed a shared list of socket numbers assigned to public services.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC divides socket numbers into general ranges, lists specific service assignments, and records which server hosts offer services.
tldr.outcome: This list superseded RFC 433 and was later replaced by RFC 739.

sections.title: What a Socket Number Identifies
sections.content:
RFC 503 is a second specification of socket numbers. It updates the list of sockets available for server hosts and adds assignments for standard, host-specific and experimental functions.

A socket number is a 40-bit quantity. Its first 8 bits specify the host, the next 24 bits are site-specific, and the last 8 bits are the AEN, or Another Eightbit Number. For the assignments in this list, the host field ranges across all hosts and the 24-bit field is zero unless specified otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: A socket number combines a host identifier with a number for a service. This list uses the service part to record the assignments shared across the network.

sections.title: Ranges and Service Assignments
sections.content:
The RFC assigns sockets 0–63 to network-wide standard functions, 64–127 to host-specific functions, 128–223 as reserved for future use, and 224–255 to experimental functions. The specific list includes Telnet at socket 1, File Transfer at 3, Remote Job Entry at 5 and Echo at 7.

It also lists socket services by host, including user-only hosts with no server sockets. The list is presented as an aid to network users, and the RFC asks readers to report missing or incorrect entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The ranges separate shared services, services specific to a host, numbers held for future use, and experimental services. The host-by-host table records which services each listed machine offers.

sections.title: Maintaining the List
sections.content:
The authors say more sockets had become available for experimental functions and that new assignments had been made. They also note that some public services used sockets that conflicted with the scheme, and hoped to resolve those conflicts with minimal disruption.

RFC 503 superseded RFC 433 according to the unit metadata, and was itself later obsoleted by RFC 739.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry was updated as assignments changed, although the RFC notes that some existing services conflicted with the scheme. RFC 739 later replaced this list.

references.text: Postel, J., "Character Generator Process," RFC 429, December 1972.
